passages.title: Problem Solving with Parallel Computing
passages.text:
**Passage A**

Recent studies have shown that sophisticated computer models of the oceans and atmosphere are capable of simulating large-scale climate trends with remarkable accuracy. But these models make use of large numbers of variables, many of which have wide ranges of possible values. Because even small differences in those values can have a significant impact on what the simulations predict, it is important to determine the impact when values differ even slightly.

Since the interactions between the many variables in climate simulations are highly complex, there is no alternative to a "brute force" exploration of all possible combinations of their values if predictions are to be reliable. This method requires very large numbers of calculations and simulation runs. For example, exhaustive examination of five values for each of only nine variables would require 2 million calculation-intensive simulation runs. Currently available individual computers are completely inadequate for such a task.

However, the continuing increase in computing capacity of the average desktop computer means that climate simulations can now be run on privately owned desktop machines connected to one another via the Internet. The calculations are divided among the individual desktop computers, which work simultaneously on their share of the overall problem. Some public resource computing projects of this kind have already been successful, although only when they captured the public's interest sufficiently to secure widespread participation.

**Passage B**

Researchers are now learning that many problems in nature, human society, science, and engineering are naturally "parallel"; that is, that they can be effectively solved by using methods that work simultaneously in parallel. These problems share the common characteristic of involving a large number of similar elements such as molecules, animals, even people, whose individual actions are governed by simple rules but, taken collectively, function as a highly complex system.

An example is the method used by ants to forage for food. As Lewis Thomas observed, a solitary ant is little more than a few neurons strung together by fibers. Its behavior follows a few simple rules. But when one sees a dense mass of thousands of ants, crowded together around their anthill retrieving food or repelling an intruder, a more complex picture emerges; it is as if the whole is thinking, planning, calculating. It is an intelligence, a kind of live computer, with crawling bits for wits.

We are now living through a great paradigm shift in the field of computing, a shift from sequential computing (performing one calculation at a time) to massive parallel computing, which employs thousands of computers working simultaneously to solve one computation-intensive problem. Since many computation-intensive problems are inherently parallel, it only makes sense to use a computing model that exploits that parallelism. A computing model that resembles the inherently parallel problem it is trying to solve will perform best. The old paradigm, in contrast, is subject to the speed limits imposed by purely sequential computing.

summaries.standard:
******Main Point (Passage A)******

The continuing increase in computing capacity of the average desktop computer means that climate simulations can now be run on privately owned desktop machines connected to one another via the Internet (Third Paragraph of Passage A).

******Passage Map (Passage A)******

****P1**** - The use of computer models to predict large-scale climate trends.
****P2**** - The computations are so intense that individual computers are inadequate.
****P3**** - Individual computers can be linked together via the Internet to run simultaneous calculations and conduct complex modeling when the public’s interest has been captured.

******Main Point (Passage B)******

We are now living through a great paradigm shift in the field of computing, a shift from sequential computing to massive parallel computing (Third Paragraph of Passage B).

******Passage Map (Passage B)******

****P1**** - Many problems are naturally parallel.
****P2**** - An example—ants.
****P3**** - Since many problems are naturally parallel, it makes sense to use parallel computing to solve them.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of passage B?

choices.text: Many difficult problems in computing are naturally parallel.
choices.explanation: This is supporting evidence, not the main point (final paragraph of passage B). Note the word “since,” indicating that this point is evidence.

choices.text: Sequential computing is no longer useful because of the speed limits it imposes.
choices.explanation: The main point not only suggests that sequential computing is not the best model for parallel problems, but that parallel computing is the best model. Furthermore, suggesting that sequential computing is not useful is too strong. There could be use cases for which sequential computing is still useful.

choices.text: There is currently a paradigm shift occurring in the field of computing toward parallel computing.
choices.explanation: The opening of passage Bs final paragraph explicitly identifies a shift from sequential to massive parallel computing. The discussion of naturally parallel problems explains the rationale for that shift.

choices.text: Complex biological and social systems are the next frontier in the field of computer simulation.
choices.explanation: The main point is that there is a new approach being used in the field of computing to examine problems like complex biological and social systems. The computational approach is new, not necessarily the fields being investigated.

choices.text: Inherently parallel computing problems are best solved by means of computers modeled on the human mind.
choices.explanation: Computers modeled on the human mind are not discussed in the passage.

questions.prompt: The large-scale climate trends discussed in passage A are most analogous to which one of the following elements in passage B?

choices.text: the thousands of computers working simultaneously to solve a calculation-intensive problem
choices.explanation: The computers in passage B are analogous to the computers in passage A—they both represent the solution used to solve the problem of complex systems.

choices.text: the simple rules that shape the behavior of a single ant
choices.explanation: The large-scale climate trends are analogous to thousands of ants acting together.

choices.text: the highly complex behavior of a dense mass of thousands of ants
choices.explanation: The large-scale climate trends discussed in passage A are an example of a complex system that require computers to model (second paragraph). This is the same for the example of ants in passage B (second paragraph of passage B).

choices.text: the paradigm shift from sequential to parallel computing
choices.explanation: The paradigm shift in passage B represents a change in the solution, while the large-scale climate trends in passage A are the problem the solution is directed at.

choices.text: the speed limits imposed by computing purely sequentially
choices.explanation: The speed limits imposed by sequential computing are the limits to the inferior solution, while the climate trends in passage A are the problem the solution is directed at.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred that the authors of the two passages would be most likely to agree on which one of the following statements concerning computing systems?

choices.text: Massive, parallel computing systems are able to solve complex computation-intensive problems without having to resort to "brute force."
choices.explanation: The author of passage A would disagree with this (second paragraph).

choices.text: Computer models are not capable of simulating the behavior of very large biological populations such as insect colonies.
choices.explanation: B uses the ant colony to illustrate naturally parallel complexity in paragraph 2, then argues in paragraph 3 for computing models that exploit such parallelism. It does not support a categorical inability to simulate large biological populations.

choices.text: Parallel computing systems that link privately owned desktop computers via the Internet are not feasible because they rely too heavily on public participation.
choices.explanation: A's paragraph 3 explicitly describes successful projects linking privately owned desktop computers, while acknowledging that participation is needed. B supplies a computational rationale for parallelism rather than a claim that public participation makes it infeasible.

choices.text: Currently available computers are not well-suited to running simulations, even if the simulated problems are relatively simple.
choices.explanation: A's paragraph 1 says sophisticated models already simulate large-scale climate trends accurately; paragraphs 2 and 3 distinguish the demands of exhaustive runs on an individual machine from distributed processing. B's paragraph 3 likewise favors parallel computing for intensive problems. Neither supports this broad rejection of currently available computers, even for simple simulations.

choices.text: Parallel computing systems employing multiple computers are the best means for simulating large-scale climate trends.
choices.explanation: A's paragraphs 1 and 2 explain the many interacting variables and demanding calculations in climate simulations, and paragraph 3 proposes linked computers working simultaneously. B's paragraph 3 says models exploiting a problem's inherent parallelism perform best. Together these support the proposed use of multiple computers for climate simulations.

questions.prompt: The author of passage A mentions public participation (final sentence of passage A) primarily in order to

choices.text: encourage public engagement in the sort of computing model discussed in the passage
choices.explanation: The author does not encourage the public to participate, but rather identifies the public as a critical factor to the computing model’s success.

choices.text: identify a factor affecting the feasibility of the computing model advocated in the passage
choices.explanation: Capturing the public interest is identified as a necessary condition of the computing model based on connected desktop machines (third paragraph).

choices.text: indicate that government support of large-scale computing efforts is needed
choices.explanation: Government support is not discussed in passage A.

choices.text: demonstrate that adequate support for the type of approach described in the passage already exists
choices.explanation: Adequate support for some similar public resource computing projects has existed, but whether it exists for modeling large-scale climate trends is not stated in passage A.

choices.text: suggest that a computing model like that proposed in the passage is infeasible because of forces beyond the designers' control
choices.explanation: The author suggests the computing model is feasible under certain conditions.

questions.prompt: Passage B relates to passage A in which one of the following ways?

choices.text: The argument in passage B has little bearing on the issues discussed in passage A.
choices.explanation: Passage B argues for a computing solution very similar to the one described in passage A.

choices.text: The explanation offered in passage B shows why the plan proposed in passage A is unlikely to be implemented.
choices.explanation: B gives a rationale for the parallel approach, not a reason implementation is unlikely. It does not guarantee implementation or public participation; those are separate from computational suitability.

choices.text: The ideas advanced in passage B provide a rationale for the solution proposed in passage A.
choices.explanation: The solution proposed in passage A is connected desktop machines working simultaneously on the problem (third paragraph), while passage B suggests that problems that are naturally parallel are best solved using a computer model that resembles the inherently parallel problem (final paragraph of passage B).

choices.text: The example given in passage B illustrates the need for the "brute force" exploration mentioned in passage A.
choices.explanation: The example given in passage B may be an example that is best studied with brute force, but does not illustrate the need for brute force since it does not suggest the vast number of calculations that would be required to model the behavior.

choices.text: The discussion in passage B conflicts with the assumptions about individual computers made in passage A.
choices.explanation: A's paragraph 2 describes the inadequacy of currently available individual computers for exhaustive climate simulations. B's paragraph 3 identifies speed limits of sequential computing and explains the benefit of many computers working simultaneously. These ideas support rather than conflict with the proposed distributed solution.

questions.prompt: The passages share which one of the following as their primary purpose?

choices.text: to show that the traditional paradigm in computing is ineffective for many common computing tasks
choices.explanation: Common computing tasks are not discussed in the passage.

choices.text: to argue that a new approach to computing is an effective way to solve a difficult type of problem
choices.explanation: A proposes connected desktops for computation-intensive climate simulations, and B argues that naturally parallel problems are best addressed through parallel computing. Both advocate the effectiveness of this approach.

choices.text: to convince skeptics of the usefulness of desktop computers for calculation-intensive problems
choices.explanation: Skeptics are not discussed in the passage.

choices.text: to demonstrate that a new computing paradigm has supplanted the traditional paradigm for most large-scale computing problems
choices.explanation: For some large-scale computing problems a new computing paradigm is superior to the traditional one, but to say it is true for most such problems goes too far.

choices.text: to describe complex and as yet unsolved problems that have recently arisen in computing
choices.explanation: The purpose is to discuss the solution to the large-scale computing problems, not the problems themselves.

questions.prompt: In calling a population of ants "an intelligence, a kind of live computer" (last sentence of the second paragraph of passage B) the author of passage B most likely means that

choices.text: the behavior of the colony of ants functions as a complex, organized whole
choices.explanation: Passage Bs second paragraph describes a colony whose many individually simple actions collectively behave as a complex, organized system. Live computer is a metaphor for that collective functioning.

choices.text: the paradigm shift taking place in computing was inspired by observations of living systems
choices.explanation: The referenced lines describe the phenomenon (problem in nature), not the means of researching that phenomenon (parallel computing).

choices.text: computers are agglomerations of elements that can be viewed as being alive in a metaphorical sense
choices.explanation: The second paragraph of passage B provides a description of ants, while this is a description of computers.

choices.text: computer simulations can simulate the behavior of large biological populations with great accuracy
choices.explanation: “Great accuracy” is stronger than the author commits to in the passage.

choices.text: the simple rules that govern the behavior of individual ants have been adapted for use in computer simulations
choices.explanation: It’s the complex picture that emerges (second paragraph of passage B) that provides the need to solve the problem with parallel computing rather than sequential computing.

questions.prompt: The author of passage B would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements regarding the computing system proposed in the last paragraph of passage A?

choices.text: It would be a kind of live computer.
choices.explanation: The author of passage B does not intend to say that computers are alive.

choices.text: It would be completely inadequate for simulating large-scale climate trends.
choices.explanation: The author of passage B believes that parallel computing makes sense (final paragraph of passage B).

choices.text: It would impose strict limitations on the number of variables that could be used in any simulation it runs.
choices.explanation: B favors parallel models for large complex systems but does not specify the maximum number of variables in As proposed system. Capacity to handle many elements does not prove that no strict limit exists.

choices.text: It would be likely to secure widespread public participation.
choices.explanation: The author of passage B does not take a position on which projects are likely to secure public participation.

choices.text: It would solve calculation-intensive problems faster than a traditional sequential computer would.
choices.explanation: This is supported in the final paragraph of passage B.

passages.title: Statutory Law
passages.text:
A proficiency in understanding, applying, and even formulating statutes—the actual texts of laws enacted by legislative bodies—is a vital aspect of the practice of law, but statutory law is often given too little attention by law schools. Much of legal education, with its focus on judicial decisions and analysis of cases, can give a law student the impression that the practice of law consists mainly in analyzing past cases to determine their relevance to a client's situation and arriving at a speculative interpretation of the law relevant to the client's legal problem.

Lawyers discover fairly soon, however, that much of their practice does not depend on the kind of painstaking analysis of cases that is performed in law school. For example, a lawyer representing the owner of a business can often find an explicit answer as to what the client should do about a certain tax-related issue by consulting the relevant statutes. In such a case the facts are clear and the statutes' relation to them transparent, so that the client's question can be answered by direct reference to the wording of the statutes. But statutes' meanings and their applicability to relevant situations are not always so obvious, and that is one reason that the ability to interpret them accurately is an essential skill for law students to learn.

Another skill that teaching statutory law would improve is synthesis. Law professors work hard at developing their students' ability to analyze individual cases, but in so doing they favor the ability to apply the law in particular cases over the ability to understand the interrelations among laws. In contrast, the study of all the statutes of a legal system in a certain small area of the law would enable the student to see how these laws form a coherent whole. Students would then be able to apply this ability to synthesize in other areas of statutory law that they encounter in their study or practice. This is especially important because most students intend to specialize in a chosen area, or areas, of the law.

One possible argument against including training in statutory law as a standard part of law school curricula is that many statutes vary from region to region within a nation, so that the mastery of a set of statutes would usually not be generally applicable. There is some truth to this objection; law schools that currently provide some training in statutes generally intend it as a preparation for practice in their particular region, but for schools that are nationally oriented, this could seem to be an inappropriate investment of time and resources. But while the knowledge of a particular region's statutory law is not generally transferable to other regions, the skills acquired in mastering a particular set of statutes are, making the study of statutory law an important undertaking even for law schools with a national orientation.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

Statutory law and why law schools should emphasize it more in legal education.

**Framework**

Challenge Position (the author pushes back against the way most law schools under-emphasize statutory law)

**Main Point**

Law schools focus too much on judicial decisions and case analysis, often neglecting statutory law, but developing skills related to statutes is essential for legal practice, making statutory law a crucial part of legal education even if statutes differ regionally. (The Most Valuable Sentence for the main point appears in the opening sentence and is fleshed out in the final sentence of the passage.)

**P1: Law School’s Emphasis on Judicial Decisions**

Many law schools tend to focus their teaching on analyzing past court cases, which can give students the wrong impression that legal practice is mostly about interpreting case law rather than directly using or understanding statutes (laws written by legislatures).

**P2: The Importance of Statutes in Legal Practice**

In real legal work, lawyers often need to consult statutes directly to answer clients’ questions, and while sometimes using statutes is straightforward, accurately interpreting them when things aren’t clear is a vital legal skill.

**P3: Teaching Statutory Law Develops Synthesis Skills**

Teaching statutory law helps students become better at seeing how different laws fit together as a whole, rather than just analyzing one case at a time—a valuable ability, especially since most law students eventually specialize.

**P4: Addressing the Objection about Regional Differences in Statutes**

Some might argue that because statutes vary by region, spending time on them in law school isn’t useful for everyone. The author admits there’s some truth to this, but clarifies that while knowledge of specific regional statutes may not transfer, the skills gained from learning statutory law are useful everywhere.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The central topic is this passage was "learning about statutes".

Why was the author writing about it? What was her purpose? What Framework did we use?

The author was doing a *Problem / Solution* kind of thing. She was arguing that it's a Problem that mastery of statutes is "a vital aspect of the practice of law but is often given too little attention by law schools".

What's her Solution?

Teach students more about statutory law!

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Let's look for something that sounds like, "It's a Problem that we don't teach students enough about statutes (emphasizing case-analysis instead)" or something more Solution-centric like, "We should teach statutory law more, since it's a vital part of real life law and it helps students with synthesis."

choices.text: In spite of the reservations that nationally oriented law schools can be expected to have, law schools can serve the overall needs of law students better by implementing a standard national curriculum in statutory law.
choices.explanation:
The main clause of this answer is "law schools [should] implement a standard national curriculum in statutory law".

We love that its main emphasis is "let's do statutory law!", but the specifics are off. The author never called for a **standard** national curriculum.

In the final paragraph, the author is explaining that even if a statutory law curriculum at a regional law school is only dealing with local laws (thus, non-standardized across the country), that's still worthwhile education. The author thinks that law students can transfer the skills they learned while studying the laws of the state where they attend law school to the statutory law in whatever state where they end up practicing law.

choices.text: Since the skills promoted by the study of statutory law are ultimately more important than those promoted by case analysis, the relative emphasis that law schools place on these two areas should be reversed.
choices.tag: Too Strong: reverse emphasis / Unsupported: more important
choices.explanation:
This is also close to the correct sentiment, because it's saying that law schools should place more emphasis on statutory law than they currently do.

But it gets a little too loaded and specific with its language.

Did the author say that the skills of statutory law are **more important** than those of case law?

No, she says that the skills of statutory law are "a vital aspect" of the practice of law, but she doesn't directly compare them in importance to the skills of case law.

Also, she says that law schools "often give too little attention" to statutory law. She believes that law schools "should give more attention to statutory law **than they currently do**", but she never says that "law schools should give more attention to statutory law **than they give to case law**".

choices.text: Although statutes typically vary from region to region, law schools should provide training in statutory law in order to develop students' ability to synthesize legal information and interpret individual statutes.
choices.explanation:
The main clause is that "law schools should provide training in statutory law", which is definitely in line with what we want.

Can we sign off on the rest of the details?

The answer begins with "although statutes typically vary from region to region". Is that true?

Yes, the beginning of the final paragraph talks about that. And it's brought up as a possible objection, which the author then counters. So it makes sense that in this answer choice, the possible objection is prefaced by **although**, and then countered by the main clause.

Did the author think that a big reason to teach statutory law is that it improves a student's "ability to synthesize legal information and interpret individual statutes"?

Yes, the 2nd paragraph is all about need to interpret, and the 3rd paragraph is about the skill of synthesis.

choices.text: In the theoretical world of law school training, as opposed to the actual practice of law, a proficiency in case law is often one of the most important assets that students can have.
choices.explanation:
The main clause of this answer is that "a proficiency in case law is often one of the most important assets that students can have".

The author is not worried about encouraging people to study case law. That's taken care of. The author's worried about encouraging people to study *statutory* law.

choices.text: Law schools generally are deficient in their attention to statutory law training and therefore fail to impart the skills necessary for the analysis of legal information.
choices.explanation:
This has the right main sentiment: "Law schools should teach statutory law more".

But the terms are a little overbaked.

Did the author says that **most** law schools are deficient in their attention to statutory law? (generally / typically / usually / tends to = most of the time)

No, the first sentence just says that "statutory law is **often** given too little attention by law schools".

"Often" does not mean "more than half the time". You might live in an area like Pittsburgh where you *often* have snow on Christmas, but you don't have snow on *most* Christmases.

Does the author say that this results a "failure to impart the skills necessary for the analysis of legal information"?

Not quite. This language is too black and white. The author definitely thinks that many law schools could do a *better* job at imparting useful skills lawyers need in the real world. But it's different to say that "law schools generally fail to impart skills necessary to analyze legal information".

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is cited in the passage as a reason that might be given for not including statutory law training in law school curricula?

choices.text: Such training would divert resources away from the far more important development of the ability to analyze cases.
Such training is not essentially different from what is already provided in the core areas of law school education.
The goals of such training can better be achieved by other means, most of which are more directly related to the actual practice of law.
Such training would be irrelevant for those students who do not plan to specialize.
The lack of geographic uniformity among statutory laws makes expertise in the statutes of any particular region generally nontransferable.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following would, if true, most weaken the author's argument as expressed in the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Supporting Text
explanationBlocks.body:
We need to start by expressing to ourselves, "What *was* the author's argument in the passage?"

CONCLUSION
There should be more training in law schools on statutory law

EVIDENCE
Training in interpreting statutes is important when the meaning and applicability to situation is not obvious.

Training in statutory law can help law students synthesize, i.e. understand the interrelations among laws that help the laws in a given small area to form a coherent whole.

Becoming good at mastering a set of statutes is a generalizable skill -- even if the set you learned isn't the law of the land where you practice law, your mastery of that set will help you master a new set.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
We either need to undermine the force/relevance of the author's support or find some independent reason to oppose her conclusion.

Something like
- ambiguous, tricky statutory interpretations are very rare and inconsequential
- the skill of synthesis is not one that lawyers usually need
- it is very hard to get any portable value out of mastering a set of statutes that won't apply where you practice law

Or just something that sound like,
- we *shouldn't* increase the time we spend on statutory law in law school.

choices.text: Many law school administrators recommend the inclusion of statutory law training in the curricula of their schools.
choices.explanation: This sounds more like people in agreement with the author, not weakening.

choices.text: Most lawyers easily and quickly develop proficiency in statutory law through their work experiences after law school.
choices.explanation: This sounds like an independent reason to resist the author's conclusion -- most lawyers will easily / quickly develop proficiency in statutory law as they get into the real world, so no need to waste precious law school time on it.

choices.text: Most lawyers do not practice law in the same geographic area in which they attended law school.
choices.explanation: This would be something like an objection, except for the fact that the author explicitly took this objection head-on in the last paragraph and explained why statutory expertise would be transferrable to new geographic areas.

choices.text: The curricula of many regionally oriented law schools rely primarily on analysis of cases.
choices.explanation: The fact that regional law schools are mainly doing case law is supporting our author's concern: *at regional schools, where you could actually study and master* *****that region's***** *set of laws, studying statutory law would be particularly useful*.

choices.text: Most lawyers who have undergone training in statutory law are thoroughly familiar with only a narrow range of statutes.
choices.explanation:
This sounds like something the 3rd paragraph is fully aware of. The author says "the study of all the statutes of a legal system ****in a certain small area of the law****" would nevertheless enable the students to apply this ability to synthesize in other areas of statutory law.

The author is cool with the idea that law school students would emerge with thorough knowledge on a small area of law, because she thinks they will have been exposed to proper methodologies that will guide their ability to learn other sets of statutes.

questions.prompt: The author discusses the skill of synthesis in the third paragraph primarily in order to

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
The correct answer to Local Purpose usually reinforces the broader *Framing Idea* that comes right before the detail in question (or, less commonly, the broader*Takeaway* that comes right after).

In this case, they're asking us about the entire 3rd paragraph, where the author talks about synthesis.

The opening sentence of the 3rd paragraph begins, "**Another skill** that teaching statutory law would improve is synthesis."

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: So if we're trying to connect this to a broader, earlier Framing Idea, it would sound like, "The author is discussing synthesis to build another premise onto the case he's making for teaching statutory law more strongly in law school."

choices.text: identify and describe one of the benefits that the author says would result from the change that is advocated in the passage
choices.explanation:
The purpose of a paragraph is usually revealed in its opening sentence. This 3rd paragraph began, "**Another** skill that teaching statutory law would improve is synthesis." So the paragraph is building the case that we should make sure law schools do a good job teaching statutory law.

That's the change advocated in the passage, because "statutory law is often given too little attention by law schools".

In the 2nd paragraph the author provides the first benefit of studying statutory law: sometimes the wording of the statute is ambiguous and you're unsure of its relation to your client's situation. In those nebulous situations, a keen ability to interpret statutes would be super useful.

In the 3rd paragraph the author provides the second benefit of studying statutory law: you build your ability to synthesize bodies of laws together, by better understanding the interrelations among laws.

choices.text: indicate that law schools currently value certain other skills over this skill and explain why this is so
choices.explanation: The paragraph explicitly discusses law professors favoring individual-case application over understanding interrelations among laws. It does not explain why they favor that emphasis. Its main role is to supply another benefit of statutory training, synthesis.

choices.text: argue for the greater importance of this skill as compared with certain others that are discussed earlier in the passage
choices.explanation:
The author wants to make sure statutory law isn't ignored. She isn't necessarily arguing that it's *more* important than case laws.

So we can't say she's arguing that "knowing how a system of laws interrelate (synthesis)" is a more important skill than "analyzing individual cases".

Nothing in the 3rd paragraph sounds comparative. At no point is the author saying that synthesis is more important than something else.

She frames her discussion of synthesis as simply "a 2nd benefit we could get by making sure we teach statutory law in law schools".

choices.text: explain why this skill is necessary for the study of statutory law
choices.explanation:
Nothing here would support the extreme claim that "Synthesis is **necessary** for the study of statutory law".

Also, that makes it seem like synthesis comes first, but the author was saying that studying statutory law leads to having more skill with synthesis.

choices.text: provide an example of the type of problem typically encountered in the practice of law
choices.tag: Out of Scope: example / typical problem
choices.explanation:
Nothing in the 3rd paragraph gets specific enough to qualify as an example. And the author isn't talking about any typical problem encountered in law.

The author is talking about a skill that is acquired when you're taught statutory law in law school.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following questions can be most clearly and directly answered by reference to information in the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
There nothing we can do to pre-game this sort of question. We just have to find an answer choice that is posing a question whose answer we can locate in the passage.

Ctrl/Command + F, where allowable, can be useful in terms of taking a keyword from an answer choice and then quickly finding that sentence from the passage to check on whether the answer's question was / wasn't answered.

choices.text: What are some ways in which synthetic skills are strengthened or encouraged through the analysis of cases and judicial decisions?
choices.explanation: The author contrasts the emphasis of case analysis with a proposed way to develop synthesis through statutes. The passage does not give specific ways case analysis strengthens synthesis, but it also need not imply case analysis can never develop that skill.

choices.text: In which areas of legal practice is a proficiency in case analysis more valuable than a proficiency in statutory law?
choices.explanation: The author argues that statutory training deserves more attention, without ranking the value of statutory proficiency against case analysis in specific fields. No area where case analysis is more valuable is identified.

choices.text: What skills are common to the study of both statutory law and judicial decisions?
choices.explanation:
The only skills we hear about studying statutory law are "accurate interpretation of the statutes' meanings and applicability" and "synthesis".

We only hear about "judicial decisions" in the second sentence of the passage, where the author says law school currently focuses on those and analysis of cases, rather than on statutory law.

We're never told that studying judicial decisions involves improving the skill of synthesis or of accurate interpretation of statutes' meanings.

choices.text: What are some objections that have been raised against including the study of statutes in regionally oriented law schools?
choices.tag: Too Specific: regionally oriented law schools
choices.explanation:
The only objection raised against studying statutes is that "it could seem to be an inappropriate investment of time and resources (if you're not planning to practice law in that region, because) a particular region's statutory law is not generally transferable to other regions."

This objection is targeted at law schools with a national orientation. Why would I go to Harvard and bother learning the regional statutory law of Massachusetts if most of that isn't going to transfer to Los Angeles, where I plan to practice?

But this objection isn't relevant to regionally oriented law schools. Those law schools are prepping students who plan to practice law in that particular region.

The passage presents the practice of teaching statutory law as something that is already done at regionally oriented schools, without controversy. The author is saying that statutory law should be taught at all law schools, and the objection in the final paragraph is about whether it would make sense to teach it at a nationally oriented school.

choices.text: What is the primary focus of the curriculum currently offered in most law schools?
choices.explanation: The opening describes much of legal education as focused on judicial decisions and case analysis. That general description answers the question about the primary curricular emphasis. This does not depend on treating most clearly and directly answered as permission to use a looser evidence standard.

questions.prompt: The information in the passage suggests that the author would most likely agree with which one of the following statements regarding training in statutory law?

choices.text: While nationally oriented law schools have been deficient in statutory law training, most regionally oriented law schools have been equally deficient in the teaching of case law.
Training in statutory law would help lawyers resolve legal questions for which the answers are not immediately apparent in the relevant statutes.
Lawyers who are trained in statutory law typically also develop a higher level of efficiency in manipulating details of past cases as compared with lawyers who are not trained in this way.
Courses in statutory law are less effective if they focus specifically on the statutes of a particular region or in a particular area of the law.
Lawyers who do not specialize probably have little need for training in statutory law beyond a brief introduction to the subject.

questions.prompt: Each of the following conforms to the kinds of educational results that the author would expect from the course of action proposed in the passage EXCEPT:

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Where in the passage does the author ever seem to list the expected results from teaching statutory law, as she recommends?

At outset of the 3rd paragraph, we see "****Another**** skill that teaching statutory law would improve is synthesis."

So that means that paragraph 2 apparently mentioned a skill that teaching statutory law would improve. The final sentence of paragraph 2 is saying that an education in statutory law would help a lawyer to decide in "close call" situations, where it's not immediately evident whether the language of the statute applies to a given client's situation.

In the 3rd paragraph, the skill of *synthesis* refers to the ability to better "understand the interrelations among laws". There are two more sentences with explicit promises of what statutory education would provide:

- [it] *would enable the student to see how these laws form a coherent whole*
*-* [it] *would allow the student to then apply this ability in other areas of statutory law they end up seeing later in life*

Finally, the final sentence of the passage makes one last promise:

*the skills acquired in mastering a particular set of statutes are generally transferable to other regions* (this seems to echo the last tidbit we grabbed from the 3rd paragraph).

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
Let's gather together our basket of bullet points. What does a statutory law education do for us?

- helps us judge whether a statute is applicable to a client, in tricky circumstances
- helps us with synthesis (understand interrelations among laws)
- helps us see how all laws within a legal system form a coherent whole
- helps us apply / transfer this understanding to other statutory legal systems.

Since we found 4 things and this is an EXCEPT question, the four answers to eliminate will probably match up with these, whereas the correct answer will like be a mismatched idea that applies to the status quo, not to the author's plan.

So maybe something like, "emphasis on studying individual cases"

choices.text: skill in locating references to court decisions on an issue involving a particular statute regarding taxation
choices.explanation:
Because this answer is talking about finding previous cases to cite as precedent, this answer sounds more like the status quo, in which the education is focused mainly on what cases can tell us.

But more importantly, we just don't have a line reference saying that an education in statutory law would speed up our ability to locate references.

choices.text: an understanding of the ways in which certain underlying purposes are served by an interrelated group of environmental laws
choices.explanation:
This matches the sense of "you can apply your understanding of the internal logic and coherence of *this* body of statutes to some other field you encounter in your study or practice".

It reinforces language from some of the author's promises:

- helps us judge whether a statute is applicable to a client, in tricky circumstances
- helps us with synthesis (understand ****interrelations**** among laws)
- helps us see how all laws within a legal system ****form a coherent whole****
- helps us apply / ****transfer this understanding to other**** statutory legal systems.

choices.text: a knowledge of how maritime statutes are formulated
choices.explanation:
This doesn't match any of the author's explicit promises, but the first sentence of the passage implies that if statutory law were studied more by law schools, students would develop ...

*a proficiency in understanding, applying, and even* *****formulating***** *statutes.*

There is also the chance that such an education would zoom in on maritime law, as an exemplar of a statutory body of laws (3rd paragraph):

*the study of all the statutes of a legal system* *****in a certain small area***** *of the law would enable the student to see how these laws form a coherent whole.*

I don't love this answer, because specific knowledge about maritime statutes certainly doesn't seem like a given. The author is clearly saying that a student who receives a better statutory law education would have ****the capacity**** to understand how maritime statues are formulated, but the author isn't necessarily expecting maritime law to be covered.

However, the question stem isn't saying the author expects ****this**** result, just ****this kind**** of result.

choices.text: familiarity with the specific wordings of a group of laws applying to businesses in a particular region or locality
choices.explanation:
The author expects that students subjected to more rigorous statutory law education would become more masterful about interpreting the language of statutes (end of P2), which is why "familiarity with specific wordings" seems like the type of educational result the author would expect.

At the beginning of the final paragraph, the author anticipates an objection -- "Won't it be dumb that students are just learning the statues of a given region, given that statutes vary from region to region?"

The author concedes, "Yes, statutes vary and they would only be getting *knowledge of a particular region's statutory law*. While the knowledge of that law wouldn't transfer to another region, the skills of how to master a new set of statutes would transfer."

In other words, this answer represents an educational result of studying statutory law, even though the result the author really cares about is "how to master any set of statutes", rather than "familiarity with a particular region's".

But this still conforms to the author's expectations. The question stem isn't asking for which educational results the author most highly values. Just which ones are expected.

choices.text: an appreciation of the problems of wording involved in drafting antiterrorism laws
choices.explanation:
This is a blend of (C) and (D).

You have the "certain small area of the law" (maritime, environmental, antiterrorism) as well as better understanding / proficiency / appreciation / knowledge of the intricacies of that body of law (how it was formulated or drafted / what specific wordings or problems with wordings arise).

Ultimately, the 4 conforming answers are just a fuzzy way of expressing, "Look this person is knowledgeable of statutes, sensitive to nuances, able to apply that knowledge to other bodies of statutes".

The wrong answer is focused on, "Look this person is better able to research ****court cases****."

passages.title: Sculptor Isamu Noguchi
passages.text:
The Japanese American sculptor Isamu Noguchi (1904-1988) was an artist who intuitively asked—and responded to—deeply original questions. He might well have become a scientist within a standard scientific discipline, but he instead became an artist who repeatedly veered off at wide angles from the well-known courses followed by conventionally talented artists of both the traditional and modern schools. The story behind one particular sculpture typifies this aspect of his creativeness.

By his early twenties, Noguchi's sculptures showed such exquisite comprehension of human anatomy and deft conceptual realization that he won a Guggenheim Fellowship for travel in Europe. After arriving in Paris in 1927, Noguchi asked the Romanian-born sculptor Constantin Brancusi if he might become his student. When Brancusi said no, that he never took students, Noguchi asked if he needed a stonecutter. Brancusi did. Noguchi cut and polished stone for Brancusi in his studio, frequently also polishing Brancusi's brass and bronze sculptures. Noguchi, with his scientist's mind, pondered the fact that sculptors through the ages had relied exclusively upon negative light—that is, shadows—for their conceptual communication, precisely because no metals, other than the expensive, nonoxidizing gold, could be relied upon to give off positive-light reflections.

Noguchi wanted to create a sculpture that was purely reflective. In 1929, after returning to the United States, he met the architect and philosopher R. Buckminster Fuller, offering to sculpt a portrait of him. When Fuller heard of Noguchi's ideas regarding positive-light sculpture, he suggested using chrome-nickel steel, which Henry Ford, through automotive research and development, had just made commercially available for the first time in history. Here, finally, was a permanently reflective surface, economically available in massive quantities.

In sculpting his portrait of Fuller, Noguchi did not think of it as merely a shiny alternate model of traditional, negative-light sculptures. What he saw was that completely reflective surfaces provided a fundamental invisibility of surface like that of utterly still waters, whose presence can be apprehended only when objects—a ship's mast, a tree, or sky—are reflected in them. Seaplane pilots making offshore landings in dead calm cannot tell where the water is and must glide in, waiting for the unpredictable touchdown. Noguchi conceived a similarly invisible sculpture, hidden in and communicating through the reflections of images surrounding it. Then only the distortion of familiar shapes in the surrounding environment could be seen by the viewer. The viewer's awareness of the "invisible" sculpture's presence and dimensional relationships would be derived only secondarily.

Even after this stunning discovery, Noguchi remained faithful to his inquisitive nature. At the moment when his explorations had won critical recognition of the genius of his original and fundamental conception, Noguchi proceeded to the next phase of his evolution.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

Isamu Noguchi's creative process — using a "scientist's mind" to reframe a fundamental sculptural problem and create a new kind of "positive-light" sculpture using chrome-nickel steel.

**Framework**

Highlight Noteworthy. The author celebrates Noguchi's habit of asking deeply original questions and tells the story behind one particular sculpture as typical of his creativeness.

**Main Point**

Noguchi's defining trait was an inquisitive scientist's mind that pushed him to ask deeply original questions about sculpture itself — questions that led him to invent a new genre of "positive-light" reflective sculpture, after which he kept moving on to the next phase rather than settling into a style.

**P1: Noguchi as a question-asker**

Noguchi was an artist who intuitively asked deeply original questions. He could have been a scientist; instead he became an artist who veered off at wide angles from conventionally talented artists. The story behind one sculpture typifies his creativeness.

**P2: Apprenticeship with Brancusi and the negative-light realization**

By his early twenties, Noguchi won a Guggenheim and went to Paris in 1927. After Brancusi declined to take him as a student, Noguchi became Brancusi's stonecutter, also polishing Brancusi's brass and bronze. With his "scientist's mind," Noguchi recognized that sculptors had always relied on negative light (shadows) because no metal except expensive gold gave reliable positive-light reflections.

**P3: The breakthrough — Fuller and chrome-nickel steel**

Noguchi wanted to create a purely reflective sculpture. After returning to the U.S. in 1929, he met R. Buckminster Fuller and offered to sculpt his portrait. Fuller suggested chrome-nickel steel — newly available commercially via Henry Ford's research and development. Here was a permanently reflective surface, available economically in massive quantities.

**P4: The conceptual leap**

For Noguchi, this wasn't just a shiny version of negative-light sculpture. Fully reflective surfaces produce a fundamental "invisibility" — like still water that you only notice when something is reflected in it. Seaplane pilots can't tell where dead-calm water is. Noguchi's invisible sculpture would be apprehended only through the distortion of surrounding images.

**P5: Moving on**

Even after this stunning discovery, Noguchi remained inquisitive. At the moment when the world recognized his original conception's genius, he proceeded to the next phase of his evolution.
summaries.brief:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

Noguchi's scientist-like questioning that led to a new "positive-light" sculpture genre.

**Framework**

Highlight Noteworthy.

**Main Point**

Noguchi's defining trait was an inquisitive mind that produced a new sculptural genre — and then kept evolving.

**P1: Noguchi as question-asker**

He could have been a scientist; instead he asked deeply original questions in art.

**P2: Brancusi and the realization**

While polishing Brancusi's sculptures, Noguchi realized sculptors had always relied on shadows (negative light) because reliably reflective metals were unavailable except for expensive gold.

**P3: The breakthrough material**

Fuller suggested chrome-nickel steel, newly available economically — finally a reliable reflective surface.

**P4: The conceptual leap**

Fully reflective surfaces produce invisibility — sculpture apprehended through distortions of surrounding images.

**P5: Moving on**

Even after recognition, Noguchi proceeded to the next phase.
summaries.anotherWay:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The author is telling a portrait story about the sculptor Isamu Noguchi — and what made his creative process distinctive.

**Framework**

Highlight Noteworthy. The author isn't arguing against anyone — they're celebrating Noguchi's habit of asking original questions.

**Main Point**

The simpler version: Noguchi could have been a scientist, and he brought a scientist's habit of mind to sculpture. He noticed that for thousands of years sculptors had been working with shadows because the reliable reflective exception, gold, was expensive. When chrome-nickel steel became available in the 1920s, he made fully reflective sculptures — and realized those surfaces don't just reflect, they go invisible, like still water. Then, when his work gained recognition, he moved on to whatever was next.

**P1: Who Noguchi was**

Someone who asked unusual questions and came at sculpture from odd angles.

**P2: The first big realization**

Working as Brancusi's stonecutter and polisher in Paris, Noguchi noticed something: every sculptor had always worked with shadows. Why? Because no metal except gold reflected light reliably. So sculptors had been forced into "negative light" by a material limitation — not by aesthetic choice.

**P3: The right material appears**

Buckminster Fuller pointed Noguchi to chrome-nickel steel — a new material from Henry Ford's automotive research that was permanently reflective and affordable in bulk. The material limit was gone.

**P4: Beyond just shiny**

Noguchi didn't just make a polished version of a normal sculpture. He realized fully reflective surfaces become *invisible*, like a still pond — you only see what they reflect. The sculpture would be perceived through the distortion of its surroundings.

**P5: Onward**

Even after this discovery made him famous, Noguchi didn't settle. He moved on.

questions.prompt: In saying that "no metals, other than the expensive, nonoxidizing gold, could be relied upon to give off positive-light reflections" (last sentence of the second paragraph), the author draws a distinction between

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: The contrast is durability of reflectivity. Noguchi polished brass and bronze, but these metals could not be relied on to retain positive-light reflections; nonoxidizing gold was the expensive exception. Paragraph 3 introduces affordable chrome-nickel steel as a permanently reflective surface. Use that contrast rather than confusing reflectivity with whether a material can be sculpted at all.

choices.text: a metal that can be made moderately reflective in any sculptural application and metals that can be made highly reflective but only in certain applications
choices.explanation: Gold can be made moderately reflective (even highly reflective), but bronze and brass are not described as able to be made highly reflective only in certain applications.

choices.text: a naturally highly reflective metal that was technically suited for sculpture and other highly reflective metals that were not so suited
choices.explanation: Brass and bronze are already being used for sculpture, as paragraph 2 shows. The relevant distinction is whether reflectivity lasts, not whether the metals are technically suitable for sculpture. Golds expense is a cost problem, not evidence that it cannot technically be sculpted.

choices.text: metals that can be made highly reflective but lose their reflective properties over time and a metal that does not similarly lose its reflective properties
choices.explanation: Polished metals such as brass and bronze do not reliably retain their reflective surface, while nonoxidizing gold does. Paragraph 3 reinforces the distinction by introducing chrome-nickel steel as another permanently reflective material.

choices.text: a highly reflective sculptural material that, because it is a metal, is long lasting and nonmetallic materials that are highly reflective but impermanent
choices.explanation: While gold is a highly reflective sculptural material, bronze and brass are metallic materials.

choices.text: a highly reflective metal that was acceptable to both traditional and modern sculptors and highly reflective metals whose use in sculpture was purely experimental
choices.explanation: The passage does not indicate that the use of bronze and brass was purely experimental.

questions.prompt: The passage provides information sufficient to answer which one of the following questions?

choices.text: In what way did Noguchi first begin to acquire experience in the cutting and polishing of stone for use in sculpture?
choices.explanation: The passage does not discuss how Noguchi acquired experience in the cutting and polishing of stone.

choices.text: In the course of his career, did Noguchi ever work in any art form other than sculpture?
choices.explanation: The only art form discussed in the passage is sculpture, though the passage does not say whether Noguchi remained within the form of sculpture during the entire course of his career.

choices.text: What are some materials other than metal that Noguchi used in his sculptures after ending his association with Brancusi?
choices.explanation: The passage does not discuss materials other than metal used by Noguchi after ending his association with Brancusi.

choices.text: During Noguchi's lifetime, was there any favorable critical response to his creation of a positive-light sculpture?
choices.explanation: This is supported in the fifth paragraph.

choices.text: Did Noguchi at any time in his career consider creating a transparent or translucent sculpture lighted from within?
choices.explanation: There is no mention of a transparent or translucent sculpture lighted from within mentioned in the passage.

questions.prompt: The passage offers the strongest evidence that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
This is an Author Opinion / Inference question with an *Undefined Target*.

We can remind ourselves of big author moments we remember (Noguchi was super creative / first one to use positive light / was able to make it purely reflective by using chrome-nickel steel), but otherwise we should just head into the answers and prioritize researching the weaker claims.

choices.text: Noguchi's work in Paris contributed significantly to the art of sculpture in that it embodied solutions to problems that other sculptors, including Brancusi, had sought unsuccessfully to overcome.
choices.explanation:
We have no evidence that Noguchi's work in polishing Brancusi's stones contributed significantly to sculpture.

Noguchi's influential sculpture doesn't happen until he gets back to the U.S.

Also, the passage doesn't say Brancusi (or other sculptors) were trying unsuccessfully to overcome the negative-light limitation.

choices.text: Noguchi's scientific approach to designing sculptures and to selecting materials for sculptures is especially remarkable in that he had no formal scientific training.
choices.explanation: The passage doesn't mention whether Noguchi had formal scientific training. The phrase "scientist's mind" describes a habit of inquisitive questioning, not a comment on his education.

choices.text: Despite the fact that Brancusi was a sculptor and Fuller was not, Fuller played a more pivotal role than did Brancusi in Noguchi's realization of the importance of negative light to the work of previous sculptors.
choices.explanation:
The passage gives Brancusi the role of letting Noguchi see what previous sculptors had been doing.

Noguchi, with his scientist's mind, "pondered the fact that sculptors through the ages had relied exclusively upon negative light" while polishing Brancusi's sculptures.

Fuller's contribution was the material (chrome-nickel steel), not helping Noguchi realize what previous sculptors had been doing.

This is basically flipping who deserves more credit.

choices.text: Noguchi was more interested in addressing fundamental aesthetic questions than in maintaining a consistent artistic style.
choices.explanation: The opening identifies deeply original questions as characteristic of Noguchi. The ending says that, just as his original conception gained critical recognition, he moved to the next phase of exploration. Together these support greater interest in fundamental inquiry than in maintaining one successful style. Merely observing one action rather than another would not establish a preference without that context.

choices.text: Noguchi's work is of special interest for what it reveals not only about the value of scientific thinking in the arts but also about the value of aesthetic approaches to scientific inquiry.
choices.tag: Out of Scope (aesthetic approach to science)
choices.explanation:
The passage discusses scientific thinking applied to art (Noguchi's "scientist's mind" examining sculpture's history), not aesthetic approaches applied to scientific inquiry.

The reverse direction, what art could teach science, isn't something the passage develops.

questions.prompt: In which one of the following is the relation between the two people most analogous to the relation between Ford and Noguchi as indicated by the passage?

choices.text: A building-materials dealer decides to market a new type of especially durable simulated­ wood flooring material after learning that a famous architect has praised the material.
choices.explanation: This does not include someone applying a material toward a new and novel purpose.

choices.text: An expert skier begins experimenting with the use of a new type of material in the soles of ski boots after a shoe manufacturer suggests that that material might be appropriate for that use.
choices.explanation: Ford never recommended chrome-nickel steel to Noguchi.

choices.text: A producer of shipping containers begins using a new type of strapping material, which a rock-climbing expert soon finds useful as an especially strong and reliable component of safety ropes for climbing.
choices.explanation: The relationship in both the passage and this answer is one where someone repurposes a material originally intended for another commercial practice (third paragraph).

choices.text: A consultant to a book editor suggests the use of a new type of software for typesetting, and after researching the software the editor decides not to adopt it but finds a better alternative as a result of the research.
choices.explanation: Noguchi adopted the same material as the one used by Ford (third paragraph), while in this answer the editor finds an alternative. Furthermore, while the software application is new of the purpose is not novel.

choices.text: A friend of a landscaping expert advises the use of a certain material for the creation of retaining walls and, as a result, the landscaper explores the use of several similar materials.
choices.explanation: Noguchi does not explore several similar materials to chrome-nickel steel.

questions.prompt: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following inferences?

choices.text: Prior to suggesting the sculptural use of chrome-nickel steel to Noguchi, Fuller himself had made architectural designs that called for the use of this material.
choices.explanation: The passage does not indicate whether Fuller had planned to use chrome-nickel steel in his own architectural designs.

choices.text: Noguchi believed that the use of industrial materials to create sculptures would make the sculptures more commercially viable.
choices.explanation: The passage does not indicate Noguchi’s views on the commercial viability of sculptures using industrial materials.

choices.text: Noguchi's "invisible" sculpture appears to have no shape or dimensions of its own, but rather those of surrounding objects.
choices.explanation: Noguchi’s “invisible” sculpture has shape and dimensions that are derived secondarily (fourth paragraph).

choices.text: If a positive-light sculpture depicting a person in a realistic manner were coated with a metal subject to oxidation, it would eventually cease to be recognizable as a realistic likeness.
choices.explanation: The hypothetical considered here is not addressed in the passage.

choices.text: The perception of the shape and dimensions of a negative-light sculpture does not depend on its reflection of objects from the environment around it.
choices.explanation: This is supported in the second and fourth paragraphs.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following inferences about the portrait of Fuller does the passage most strongly support?

choices.text: The material that Noguchi used in it had been tentatively investigated by other sculptors but not in direct connection with its reflective properties.
choices.explanation: The passage does not suggest that chrome-nickel steel had been investigated by other sculptors

choices.text: It was similar to at least some of the sculptures that Noguchi produced prior to 1927 in that it represented a human form.
choices.explanation: This is supported in the second paragraph.

choices.text: Noguchi did not initially think of it as especially innovative or revolutionary and thus was surprised by Fuller's reaction to it.
choices.explanation: Fuller’s reaction to his portrait by Noguchi is not discussed in the passage.

choices.text: It was produced as a personal favor to Fuller and thus was not initially intended to be noticed and commented on by art critics.
choices.explanation: The passage does not state that Noguchi produced the portrait of Fuller as a personal favor.

choices.text: It was unlike the sculptures that Noguchi had helped Brancusi to produce in that the latter's aesthetic effects did not depend on contrasts of light and shadow.
choices.explanation: The sculptures that Noguchi helped Brancusi with were produced of stone, but may have depended on contrasts of light and shadow.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following would, if true, most weaken the author's position in the passage?

choices.text: Between 1927 and 1929, Brancusi experimented with the use of highly reflective material for the creation of positive-light sculptures.
choices.explanation: This would undermine the author’s point that Noguchi was an artist who asked—and responded to—deeply original questions (first paragraph).

choices.text: After completing the portrait of Fuller, Noguchi produced only a few positive-light sculptures and in fact changed his style of sculpture repeatedly throughout his career.
choices.explanation: This supports the argument that Noguchi continued to evolve throughout his career (fifth paragraph).

choices.text: When Noguchi arrived in Paris, he was already well aware of the international acclaim that Brancusi's sculptures were receiving at the time.
choices.explanation: The author does not assume that Noguchi was ignorant of the fact that Brancusi’s sculptures were receiving international acclaim.

choices.text: Many of Noguchi's sculptures were, unlike the portrait of Fuller, entirely abstract.
choices.explanation: This supports the argument that Noguchi continued to evolve throughout his career (fifth paragraph).

choices.text: Despite his inquisitive and scientific approach to the art of sculpture, Noguchi neither thought of himself as a scientist nor had extensive scientific training.
choices.explanation: While Noguchi had a “scientist’s mind” (second paragraph), the author does not assume that Noguchi had scientific training.

passages.title: Ultimatum Game
passages.text:
In an experiment, two strangers are given the opportunity to share $100, subject to the following constraints: One person—the "proposer"—is to suggest how to divide the money and can make only one such proposal. The other person—the "responder"—must either accept or reject the offer without qualification. Both parties know that if the offer is accepted, the money will be split as agreed, but if the offer is rejected, neither will receive anything.

This scenario is called the Ultimatum Game. Researchers have conducted it numerous times with a wide variety of volunteers. Many participants in the role of the proposer seem instinctively to feel that they should offer 50 percent to the responder, because such a division is "fair" and therefore likely to be accepted. Two-thirds of proposers offer responders between 40 and 50 percent. Only 4 in 100 offer less than 20 percent. Offering such a small amount is quite risky; most responders reject such offers. This is a puzzle: Why would anyone reject an offer as too small? Responders who reject an offer receive nothing, so if one assumes—as theoretical economics traditionally has—that people make economic decisions primarily out of rational self-interest, one would expect that an individual would accept any offer.

Some theorists explain the insistence on fair divisions in the Ultimatum Game by citing our prehistoric ancestors' need for the support of a strong group. Small groups of hunter-gatherers depended for survival on their members' strengths. It is counterproductive to outcompete rivals within one's group to the point where one can no longer depend on them in contests with other groups. But this hypothesis at best explains why proposers offer large amounts, not why responders reject low offers.

A more compelling explanation is that our emotional apparatus has been shaped by millions of years of living in small groups, where it is hard to keep secrets. Our emotions are therefore not finely tuned to one-time, strictly anonymous interactions. In real life we expect our friends and neighbors to notice our decisions. If people know that someone is content with a small share, they are likely to make that person low offers. But if someone is known to angrily reject low offers, others have an incentive to make that person high offers. Consequently, evolution should have favored angry responses to low offers; if one regularly receives fair offers when food is divided, one is more likely to survive. Because one-shot interactions were rare during human evolution, our emotions do not discriminate between one-shot and repeated interactions. Therefore, we respond emotionally to low offers in the Ultimatum Game because we instinctively feel the need to reject dismal offers in order to keep our self-esteem. This self-esteem helps us to acquire a reputation that is beneficial in future encounters.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The Ultimatum Game and why people often reject unfair offers, even at their own expense.

**Framework**

Answer / Explain

**Main Point**

People instinctively reject low, "unfair" offers in the Ultimatum Game not because it’s the most rational economic choice, but because our emotional responses have been shaped by social evolution—rejecting poor offers preserves self-esteem and builds a reputation that is valuable in social groups. ****The Most Valuable Sentence:**** The last few sentences of the final paragraph: "Therefore, we respond emotionally to low offers in the Ultimatum Game because we instinctively feel the need to reject dismal offers in order to keep our self-esteem. This self-esteem helps us to acquire a reputation that is beneficial in future encounters."

**P1-P2: Introduction to the Ultimatum Game and Puzzle**

We’re introduced to the Ultimatum Game, where one person proposes a way to split $100, and the other must accept or reject it—with rejection meaning both get nothing. Most people tend to offer close to 50-50 splits, and it's puzzling that responders often reject very low offers, even though taking any money would be strictly “rational.”

**P3: Hypothesis About Fairness and Social Groups**

Some theorists think this desire for fairness comes from our evolutionary past in small, interdependent groups. Fairness helped groups survive, but this idea mainly explains why the proposer tries to be fair—it doesn't explain why a responder would give up money by rejecting a bad deal.

**P4: Explanation Based on Emotional Evolution**

The author provides a deeper explanation: our emotions evolved in environments where reputation mattered, and everyone’s actions were noticed. Rejecting poor offers is a way to defend our self-respect and protect our reputation, which pays off in repeated social interactions—even though the Ultimatum Game is a one-shot scenario.

**End of P4: Why We Reject Low Offers**

The passage concludes that our reactions to unfair offers are driven by a deep-set instinct to value self-esteem and reputation, which historically helped us secure better treatment in our social circles. The proposed explanation is that our emotions do not distinguish the interaction types, even in a one-time, anonymous game.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately summarizes the main idea of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Supporting Text
explanationBlocks.body:
With Main Point we find supporting text by asking a few questions:
- as we read, we did we note any Most Valuable Sentence(s)?
- what was the Purpose / Framework we used? For that framework, what is the Payoff idea? (The setup idea is optional -- the payoff idea is mandatory).

In this passage I would have been using an Explain Curious Phenomenon framework, since in P1 the author asks a question.

Any time an author asks a question, it's almost always the central purpose of the passage.

The Payoff idea when you ask a question is the Answer/Explanation. The author first considers in P2 an explanation she ultimately doesn't favor.

Then the beginning of P3 indicates that she has an explanation she likes more. The second to last sentence announces the distilled form of this preferred explanation.

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: We want an answer that sounds like that second to last sentence.

choices.text: Contrary to a traditional assumption of theoretical economics, the behavior of participants in the Ultimatum Game demonstrates that people do not make economic decisions out of rational self-interest.
choices.explanation:
The Ultimatum Game might be an instance in which people seem to act against their self-interest (although the emotional explanation the author cites would have been in a person's rational self-interest back when humans lived in nomadic tribes).

But even if this experiment shows *a time* in which people seem to not act out of rational self-interest, the author was never trying to make a strong, sweeping claim that *people do not make economic decisions out of rational self-interest*.

More importantly, this doesn't sound like the second to last sentence of the passage. This answer is telling us what people's reaction to the low offer *isn't*. The main point happens at the end of the passage, when it tells us what people's reaction to the low offer *is*.

choices.text: Although the reactions most commonly displayed by participants in the Ultimatum Game appear to conflict with rational self-interest, they probably result from a predisposition that had evolutionary value.
choices.explanation:
The warm-up clause gives us the Setup of this passage (the Curious Phenomenon). The main clause gives us the author's preferred Explanation. The first sentence of the last paragraph sounds a lot like this:

*our emotional apparatus has been shaped by millions of years of living in small groups*

Evolutionary value is shaped over millions of years. The "predisposition" refers to the language from the second to last sentence: *we respond emotionally to low offers because we instinctively need to keep our self-esteem*.

The last sentence explains that this instinctive predisposition is "beneficial in future encounters".

choices.text: Because our emotional apparatus has been shaped by millions of years of living in small groups in which it is hard to keep secrets, our emotions are not finely tuned to one-shot, anonymous interactions.
choices.explanation: This grabs language from the last paragraph, but it misses the central topic of the whole passage: *people's curious response to low offers in the Ultimatum Game.*

choices.text: People respond emotionally to low offers in the Ultimatum Game because they instinctively feel the need to maintain the strength of the social group to which they belong.
choices.explanation: This answer is focused on the right Setup, but it gets the Payoff wrong --- it's making it seem like the main point was the explanation in the *second* paragraph, that the author didn't think was as compelling as the explanation she offers in the final paragraph.

choices.text: When certain social and evolutionary factors are taken into account, it can be seen that the behavior of participants in the Ultimatum Game is motivated primarily by the need to outcompete rivals.
choices.explanation:
The author is definitely not saying, in those final two conclusory sentences, that the answer to our riddle is "it's all about outcompeting rivals".

Instead, the answer to our riddle is, "It's all about not looking like a sucker that people can take advantage of".

questions.prompt: The passage implies that the Ultimatum Game is

choices.text: one that requires two strangers to develop trust in each other
responsible for overturning a basic assumption of theoretical economics
a situation that elicits unpredictable results
a type of one-shot, anonymous interaction
proof that our emotional apparatus has been shaped by millions of years of living in small groups

questions.prompt: The author's primary purpose in the passage is to

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
