Our pre-phrase to Primary Purpose is usually heavily influenced by (or identical to) the Framework we used.

In this passage, we probably used an *Answer a Question* framework. The passage begins by describing an experiment, and then once they start telling us in the 2nd paragraph the typical trends that happen as they run the experiment, we here this:

*This is a puzzle: Why would anyone reject an offer as too small*?

When RC passages ask a question, it's usually central to the main purpose. If there is a puzzling phenomenon (a "curious fact", as we call it in LR), then explaining that phenomenon or evaluating other people's explanations for that phenomenon is usually the central purpose.

In this passage, do we get an answer to the question of why people might reject an offer as too small? (in other words, why would they turn down a 90/10 split when accepting it means they get $10 and refusing it means they get $0?)

In the 3rd paragraph the author presents "some theorists' answer" to this question, but then in the 4th paragraph she volunteers her own:

*A **more compelling** explanation is .*

The rest of that final paragraph fleshes out her explanation.

So let's look for some answer choice like
- answer a puzzling question
- provide an explanation to a confusing experimental phenomenon

choices.text: survey existing interpretations of the puzzling results of an experiment
choices.explanation: The passage considers two explanations but evaluates them unequally, favoring one that accounts for rejection of low offers. Simply calling the purpose a survey leaves out that explanatory commitment. A survey need not always be neutral or contain more than two views; the issue is the main work done here.

choices.text: show how two theories that attempt to explain the puzzling results of an experiment complement each other
choices.tag: Out of Scope: complement each other
choices.explanation:
There are two theories presented: the one in the 3rd paragraph from "some theorists" and the one in the 4th paragraph from our author.

Our author isn't saying, "My theory complements this other theory".

The author is saying, "Their theory at best explains a different part of the experimental results. But it doesn't explain the question we're trying to answer. Here's *my* theory, which is a **more compelling** explanation."

choices.text: argue that the results of an experiment, while puzzling, are valid
choices.explanation:
The author is never trying to convince the reader that the results of an experiment are valid. No one was ever challenging the validity of the results.

People were trying to explain why the results were occurring. And the author's central purpose was to offer her explanation for the why the results of this experiment are what they are.

choices.text: offer a plausible explanation for the puzzling results of an experiment
choices.explanation: The author describes the game and its puzzling rejections, identifies a limitation in the group-strength explanation, and offers the emotional-evolution explanation as more compelling. This supplies a plausible explanation of the results. Calling one explanation more compelling need not mean the other is wholly implausible.

choices.text: defend an experiment against criticism that methodological flaws caused its puzzling results
choices.explanation:
Nothing in the passage is ever suggesting that this experiment has been accused of methodological flaws.

The author isn't trying to defend an experiment; she's trying to offer an explanation for one of its puzzling results.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following sentences would most logically conclude the final paragraph of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
It's notoriously hard to predict ****Add to Passage**** answers, so we just remind ourselves of what big point we were making at the end of the passage.

The author is wrapping up his preferred response to the Ultimatum Game paradox. He thinks the best explanation for why people reject low offers is an evolutionary one based on the concept that we don't want to look like a sucker who is okay being treated unfairly, because otherwise we expect that people will learn they can take advantage of us and do so.

We want to be wary of answers that water down or backtrack from the author's main point, or answers that seem to open up a new topic that would start a new paragraph, not wrap things up. A lot of times correct answers "bookend" the passage -- they have some language that harkens back to how the passage was set up in the beginning.

choices.text: Contrary to the assumptions of theoretical economics, human beings do not act primarily out of self-interest.
choices.explanation:
The author wouldn't say that "humans don't act out of self-interest" because the explanation he favors *is* one centered around self-interest.

People reject low-offers out of self-interest: they think that it's in their long term interest to not look like a sucker who's willing to be treated unfairly.

choices.text: Unfortunately, one-time, anonymous interactions are becoming increasingly common in contemporary society.
choices.explanation:
The author has never said anything about what's becoming more common in contemporary society. This whole passage has dealt with a highly artificial research setting, and otherwise with our evolutionary past.

So this kind of "unfortunately" is adding an unsupported new dimension to the passage.

choices.text: The instinctive urge to acquire a favorable reputation may also help to explain the desire of many proposers in the Ultimatum Game to make "fair" offers.
choices.explanation:
This adds on to the same evolutionary explanation for the "responder" and loops back to make the same explanation work for the "proposer" as well.

When the author transitioned out of the 2nd and into the 3rd paragraph, she was saying "This explanation that some people pose *at best* could explain the behavior of the Proposer, but it wouldn't explain the Responder at all."

Since she then spends her 3rd paragraph describing how her preferred explanation can make sense of the Responder's behavior, it's a sensible last sentence for her to say, "Oh yeah, and it also works for the Proposer too."

Mainly, correct answers on Add to Passage are correct because the others were wrong.

choices.text: High self-esteem and a positive reputation offer individuals living in small groups many other benefits as well.
choices.explanation:
This isn't terrible, but it's more along the lines of opening up a new topic then it is looping back to wrap up loose ends or putting a bookend on the passage.

The only relevant benefit of self-esteem to this passage is the fact that people are less likely to make you low offers in the future, if you've established that you have too much self-esteem to even consider so insulting an offer.

Bringing up other benefits isn't really germane to the conversation, and we don't know what these benefits are, so this answer feels more like it would be opening up a new topic.

choices.text: The behavior of participants in the Ultimatum Game sheds light on the question of what constitutes a "fair" division.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: new concept of "fair"
choices.explanation: The passage reports that many proposers treat equal division as fair, but its explanatory target is behavior, not a definition of fairness. It does not reveal what every low-offer proposer privately regards as fair or what those proposers assume will be accepted.

questions.prompt: In the context of the passage, the author would be most likely to consider the explanation in the third paragraph more favorably if it were shown that

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
The question stem is saying, "The author would be more likely to have a positive attitude about X if which of the following were true?"

Usually, this means that we search the passage for why the author had a negative attitude about X ("it's because of reason Y").

Then, we expect the correct answer to *Flip It.*

So why didn't the author like the explanation in the 3rd paragraph? The last sentence says:

*But this hypothesis **at best** explains why proposers offer large amounts, not why responders reject low offers.*

So the author's unfavorable review is because the hypothesis only explained one of our two mysteries.

It offers an answer to the question of, "Why do people usually offer a 50/50 or 60/40 split? Why don't they just go 90/10 since they're in charge of deciding how much money they would get?"

But it doesn't offer an answer to the question of, "Why do people turn down 90/10 offers? They just end up $10 poorer than they would be if they accepted the offer?"

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
So the correct answer should give the *Flipped* version. We need for this hypothesis in the 3rd paragraph to be **able** to offer an explanation for that second question.

Let's find an answer that connects "it's counterproductive to outcompete your rivals since they will be your allies in battle" to the idea of "turning down a 90/10 offer, even though you'd get more cash by accepting the offer than by rejecting it".

choices.text: our prehistoric ancestors often belonged to large groups of more than a hundred people
choices.explanation:
Whether it's 50 people, 100, 200, what does that matter?

We need a way to argue that "the fact that we evolved in groups where it would be bad to outcompete your rivals to the point of harming them" can also explain why responders in the study turn down really small offers.

This answer doesn't connect those two at all.

choices.text: in many prehistoric cultures, there were hierarchies within groups that dictated which allocations of goods were to be considered fair and which were not
choices.explanation:
This answer is saying that some cultures had hierarchies that decided which divisions were fair or not. It's unclear whether this is saying "some cultures had authority figures who decreed whether an allocation was fair" or whether it's saying "some cultures had different tiers of economic classes, and so what was fair in one group might be unfair in other group".

Regardless, neither one of those interpretations would have anything to do with our goal of arguing that "the fact that we evolved in groups where it would be bad to outcompete your rivals to the point of harming them" can also explain why responders in the study turn down really small offers.

choices.text: it is just as difficult to keep secrets in relatively large social groups as it is in small social groups
choices.explanation: Keeping secrets is explicitly discussed in paragraph 4 as part of the authors preferred reputation explanation. This option extends that fact to larger groups, but does not address why the different group-strength explanation in paragraph 3 would predict rejecting low offers.

choices.text: it is just as counterproductive to a small social group to allow oneself to be outcompeted by one's rivals within the group as it is to outcompete those rivals
choices.explanation:
This helps us with our goal of arguing that "the fact that we evolved in groups where it would be bad to outcompete your rivals to the point of harming them" can also explain why responders in the study turn down really small offers.

The 3rd paragraph used this fact to explain why proposers in the study usually offer fair divisions: *they offer fair divisions because they want their rivals to still be adequately strong; it's counterproductive to outcompete rivals to the point of harming them, since you want their help in battles against common enemies.*

The author said, "yeah, but this fact doesn't explain why responders reject low offers". And this answer is saying, yes it does:

Responders reject low offers because that would be analogous to allowing yourself to be outcompeted by your rival.

Just as we are instinctively programmed to avoid badly outcompeting our rivals (which explains why proposers offer fair divisions), so too are we instinctively programmed to avoid being badly outcompeted by our rivals (which explains why responders reject low offers).

choices.text: in many social groups, there is a mutual understanding among the group's members that allocations of goods will be based on individual needs as opposed to equal shares
choices.explanation:
This answer makes it clear that sometimes people will tolerate unequal divisions because the people in question have very unequal needs.

This wouldn't apply at all to the Ultimatum Game, though, since the people know nothing about each other's needs.

And this has nothing to do with connecting the concept from the 3rd paragraph (you don't want to outcompete your rivals so badly that you hurt them) to why responders reject low offers.
